notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on 2 Chronicles 8, drawn from the sources found:

---

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter parallels 1 Kings 9:10–28 and covers four main sections: Solomon's city-building (vv. 1–6), forced labour from conquered peoples (vv. 7–10), the relocation of Pharaoh's daughter (v. 11), the regulation of temple worship (vv. 12–16), and the voyage to Ophir (vv. 17–18). Keil & Delitzsch note that the two accounts are "mutually supplementary extracts from a more elaborate description" — Kings adds details the Chronicler omits, and vice versa.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-chronicles-8.html

Martin Selman (cited at Precept Austin) observes that the real subject of chs. 8–9 is "what God achieved through Solomon, rather than Solomon’s own achievements."

— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-8-commentary

---

## v. 1 — "Now at the end of the twenty years during which Solomon had built the house of the LORD and his own palace"

The twenty years are reckoned from the start of temple construction: seven years for the temple (1 Kings 6:38) and thirteen for the palace (1 Kings 7:1). David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that at this point Solomon's kingdom was "secure, stable, and blessed."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-8/

Keil & Delitzsch treat v. 2 as the apodosis of v. 1: "at the end of twenty years … Solomon rebuilt the cities." The unusual word order results from the aphoristic character of the notice.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-chronicles-8.html

---

## v. 2 — "Solomon rebuilt the cities Hiram had given him and settled Israelites there"

There is a well-known difficulty: 1 Kings 9:11–14 says Solomon *gave* these cities to Hiram (who was displeased with them). Ellicott says the discrepancy is "probably because they had been returned to Solomon, either because they were unacceptable (1 Kings 9:12-13) or because they had been collateral for a loan." The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary adds that Hiram, finding them "unsuitable to the commercial habits of his people," returned them.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/8.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-8.html

The Hebrew verb *bānâ* here does not mean to build from scratch but to repair or fortify; the cities were "in very bad condition" (Keil & Delitzsch). Solomon also transplanted Israelites there to extend Judah's secure footprint northward.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-chronicles-8.html
— https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/2_chronicles/8.htm

---

## v. 3 — "Then Solomon went to Hamath-zobah and captured it"

This detail is omitted in 1 Kings. Keil & Delitzsch explain that Hamath-zobah is not a city but "the land or kingdom of Hamath," which bordered the kingdom of Zobah. David had previously made these kingdoms tributary (1 Chron 18:3–10). The phrase "prevailed against it" (Hebrew *ḥāzaq ʿal*) suggests these tributary kingdoms had either rebelled or attempted to do so, and Solomon suppressed the rebellion.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-chronicles-8.html

Matthew Henry adds simply: "Solomon went to Hamath-zobah, and prevailed against it."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-chronicles-8.html

---

## v. 4 — "He built Tadmor in the wilderness, in addition to all the store cities that he had built in Hamath"

Tadmor is identified as the famous Palmyra ("city of palms"), located on the traders' route between the Mediterranean coast and Thapsacus on the Euphrates. Ellicott notes that "Solomon was the founder of Palmyra is the tradition of the country to this day." The Pulpit Commentary says the name of Tadmor "will never be forgotten" and that its splendid ruins remained visible for centuries.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/8.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-8.html

Keil & Delitzsch say Solomon fortified Tadmor "in order to establish his dominion over them" (Hamath-Zobah), since "he had Rezon of Zobah as an enemy during his whole reign" (cf. 1 Kings 11:23ff).

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-chronicles-8.html

Haydock's Catholic Commentary identifies Tadmor with the later Emesa on the Orontes.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-8.html

---

## vv. 5–6 — Upper and Lower Beth-horon, Baalath, store cities, chariot cities

The two Beth-horons were ancient Ephraimite cities (Josh 16:3–5), now fortified "with walls, gates, and bars." Ellicott notes the parallel in 1 Kings 9:17 mentions "Gezer, and Beth-horon the nether" but omits Upper Beth-horon. Baalath was a Danite town (Josh 19:44), situated west of Jerusalem as a bulwark against the Philistines.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/8.htm

David Guzik (Enduring Word) makes a pointed application: Solomon's building of "chariot cities and the cities of the cavalry" reveals a concerning shift away from trust in God. Deuteronomy 17:16 specifically forbade Israel's kings from multiplying horses. Guzik says, "It would have been much better if Solomon had possessed the heart reflected in Psalm 20:7: *Some trust in chariots, and some in horses; but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.*"

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-8/

Matthew Henry commends Solomon's industry: though a man of great learning, "he spent his days, not in contemplation, but in action … in a time of peace preparing for a time of war." He also notes Solomon "knew how to set bounds to his desires … he finished all he desired, and then he desired no more."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-chronicles-8.html

---

## vv. 7–8 — The forced labour of the Canaanites

These verses address the remaining populations of the Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites — peoples Israel had failed to destroy. Solomon conscripted them for forced labour (*mas*), "as they are to this day." Ellicott notes that 1 Kings uses the fuller expression *mas ʿōbēd*, "tribute of labourers."

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/8.htm

Keil & Delitzsch explain that the Hebrew *min-bənêhem* in v. 8 is not partitive ("some of their sons") but refers to "those of their sons who had remained in the land, whom the Israelites had not exterminated."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-chronicles-8.html

The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary describes them as "treated as war-prisoners, employed in vast building operations, and had to pay tribute."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-8.html

---

## vv. 9–10 — Israelites not enslaved; the 250 supervisors

Israelites were not made slaves but served as "men of war," officers, captains, commanders of chariots and cavalry, and as the 250 chief supervisors (*śārê nəṣîbîm*). Keil & Delitzsch note that the number 250 (here) differs from the 550 in 1 Kings 9:23 because the 550 includes both Israelite and Canaanite upper overseers, while the Chronicler counts only the Israelite ones.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-chronicles-8.html

Haydock makes the same point: "These were different from the 550 overseers, 3 Kings ix. 23."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-8.html

Guzik notes that Israelites were used for temple and palace construction but "they were not forced labor … They were often used in the management of the forced labor."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-8/

---

## v. 11 — Solomon moves Pharaoh's daughter out of the City of David

This is one of the most commented-upon verses in the chapter. Solomon built a separate palace for his Egyptian wife and moved her out of the "City of David" because "the places the ark of the LORD has entered are holy."

**Traditional/evangelical reading:** David Guzik says this marriage "was the first of Solomon's many unwise marriages" and "launched the spiritual downfall of Solomon." G. Campbell Morgan (quoted by Guzik) says: "To build a house for Pharaoh's daughter outside the Holy City is to open its gates sooner or later to Pharaoh's gods." F.B. Meyer (also quoted) adds: "The blessedness of the marriage tie depends on whether the twain are one in spirit … Nothing is more terrible than when either admits in the secrecy of the heart, concerning the other, My husband or my wife cannot accompany me into the holy places."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-8/

Adam Clarke (cited by Guzik) asks: "Is not this a proof that he considered his wife to be a heathen, and not proper to dwell in a place which had been sanctified? Solomon had not yet departed from the true God." John Trapp (also cited) says Solomon married her "for politic ends … as hoping that by his wisdom he could reclaim them."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-8/

Matthew Henry takes a somewhat different angle: he suggests the real problem may have been her court's "great vanity" and possibly idolatrous servants, and that Solomon "so far consulted the honour of his father's memory that he would not suffer that place to be thus profaned where the ark of God had been and where holy David had prayed many a good prayer." Henry adds the important caveat: "Not that all the places where the ark had been were so holy as never to be put to a common use."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-chronicles-8.html

**Catholic reading:** Haydock notes it "was deemed improper for a pagan woman to reside in the same place" and suggests she "had perhaps pretended, at first, to be converted, but had lately given some signs of relapse." Another Catholic comment (Worthington, cited by Haydock) observes: "Solomon was as yet far from communicating with infidels."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-8.html

Keil & Delitzsch treat the verse more matter-of-factly: the remark is introduced here "because it belongs to the history of Solomon's buildings," though it comes abruptly in the Chronicle since the Chronicler had not previously mentioned the marriage. Solomon "could not allow her, an Egyptian, to dwell in the palace of King David, which had been sanctified by the reception of the ark."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-chronicles-8.html

---

## v. 12 — "Solomon offered burnt offerings to the LORD on the altar … in front of the portico"

"At that time" (*ʾāz*) means after the temple was finished and dedicated (Keil & Delitzsch). Matthew Henry emphasises: "The building of the temple was in order to the service of the temple. Whatever cost he was at in rearing the structure, if he had neglected the worship … it would all have been to no purpose."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-chronicles-8.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-chronicles-8.html

Ellicott notes that "offered" here means "not once, but habitually; according to the prescriptions of the Mosaic Law."

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/8.htm

---

## v. 13 — Daily, Sabbath, New Moon, and festival offerings

Solomon observed the daily requirement "according to the commandment of Moses" — the morning and evening sacrifices (Numbers 28:1–8) — plus offerings for Sabbaths, New Moons, and the three annual pilgrimage feasts: Unleavened Bread (Passover), Weeks (Pentecost), and Tabernacles.

Keil & Delitzsch give a technical note: the Hebrew phrasing uses the *b essentiae* ("consisting in the daily rate to sacrifice"), and the infinitive *lĕhaʿălôt* stands in place of the infinitive absolute, reflecting later Hebrew usage.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-chronicles-8.html

Matthew Henry: "There were daily sacrifices, a certain rate every day, as duly as the day came … Those are spiritual sacrifices that are now required of us, which we are to bring daily and weekly; and it is good to be in a settled method of devotion."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-chronicles-8.html

---

## v. 14 — Solomon follows David's ordinances for priests, Levites, and gatekeepers

Solomon appointed the priestly divisions (1 Chron 24), the Levites for praise and service (1 Chron 23, 25), and gatekeepers (1 Chron 26) — all "according to the order of David his father." David is here called "the man of God," a title Matthew Henry says places David alongside Moses "because he was both instructed and authorised of God to make these establishments."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-chronicles-8.html

Henry adds that "Solomon, though a wise and great man and the builder of the temple, did not attempt to amend, alter, or add to what the man of God had, in God's name, commanded, but closely adhered to that."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-chronicles-8.html

---

## v. 15 — "They did not turn aside from the king's command"

The priests and Levites faithfully carried out the king's commands regarding temple service and the treasuries (1 Chron 26:20–28). Keil & Delitzsch note that the verb *sûr* is construed here with an accusative, meaning "to transgress a command."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-chronicles-8.html

Matthew Henry says tersely: "He observed God's laws, and then all obeyed his orders."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-chronicles-8.html

---

## v. 16 — "Thus all the work of Solomon was carried out … So the house of the LORD was completed"

This verse serves as a literary conclusion to the entire temple narrative that began in 2 Chronicles 2:1. Keil & Delitzsch explain that "the day" (*hayyôm*) refers to the day when regular public worship commenced after the temple's dedication. Only then was Solomon's temple work "completed," and the house of God was *šālēm* — "integer, perfect in all its parts, as it should be."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-chronicles-8.html

Dr. Constable (cited at StudyLight) notes: "This verse represents an important literary mark in the story of the Chronicler, concluding the long section that began at 2 Chronicles 2:1. A similar phrase … occurs in 2 Chronicles 29:35, as the Chronicler concluded his account of the restoration of the temple service under Hezekiah."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-8.html (from search excerpt)

Matthew Henry: "The work was the main matter, not the place; the temple was unfinished till all this was done."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-chronicles-8.html

Iain Kunkel (cited at Precept Austin) notes that vv. 1 and 16 form a literary frame, suggesting that "the central purpose of all was to support the building and ongoing maintaining of the 'house of the Lord' and the worship there."

— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-8-commentary

---

## v. 17 — "Then Solomon went to Ezion-geber and to Eloth on the coast of Edom"

Ezion-geber and Eloth (Elath) were ports at the northern end of the Gulf of Aqaba (the Red Sea), providing strategic commercial access southward. The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary notes that Solomon visited both ports "before determining at which he should establish his docks."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-8.html

David Guzik comments that this was "unusual for an Israelite king because the people of Israel were not known for their accomplishments at sea. Solomon boldly led the people of Israel into new ventures."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-8/

Matthew Henry: "He did himself in person visit the sea-port towns … for those that deal much in the world will find it their interest, as far as they can, to inspect their affairs themselves."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-chronicles-8.html

---

## v. 18 — Hiram's ships and the 450 talents of gold from Ophir

Hiram (Huram) of Tyre supplied ships and experienced Phoenician sailors. Adam Clarke (cited by Guzik) notes that "the Jews, at no period of their history, had any skill in maritime affairs, their navigation being confined to the lakes of their own country."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-8/

Ellicott discusses the logistical question of how the Tyrian ships reached Ezion-geber: he suggests the most natural reading is that the ships sailed from Tyre to Joppa, where "a portion of their crews proceeded, by Solomon's order, to Ezion-geber." The Tyrian vessels may have been left at Joppa, avoiding the difficulty of transporting ships overland across the desert.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/8.htm

**The location of Ophir** is uncertain. Clarke lists two possibilities: one in India beyond the Ganges, another in Arabia near the Sabaeans (Job 22:24). Keil & Delitzsch conclude Ophir is "not to be sought in India, but in Southern Arabia." The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary notes Ophir was the name of a son of Joktan (Gen 10:29) and was "at least originally in the south of Arabia, though some look for it in India or Ceylon."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-chronicles-8.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-8.html

**The 450 talents**: 1 Kings 9:28 says 420 talents. Haydock suggests the extra 30 "were expended in the voyage." The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says the 450 may represent "the result of many voyages to this land." Haydock also notes the Hebrew letters for twenty and fifty are very similar, suggesting a possible scribal issue.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-8.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-8.html

Matthew Henry closes with a devotional reflection: "Canaan was a rich country, and yet must send to Ophir for gold … This teaches us that grace, and not gold, is the best riches, and acquaintance with God and his law, not with arts and sciences, the best knowledge."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-chronicles-8.html

---

## Summary of Distinctive Traditions

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Emphasises the spiritual warnings — Solomon's chariot cities as a violation of Deut 17:16, his marriage to Pharaoh's daughter as "the beginning of his spiritual downfall," and the lesson that "outward success and spiritual obedience are not the same thing." Strong application-oriented reading aimed at personal holiness.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-8/

**Reformed/Puritan (Matthew Henry):** Focuses on Solomon's industry, wisdom in setting bounds to desire, and the primacy of worship over mere building. Henry sees Solomon's scruple about his wife's residence as a partial (if insufficient) exercise of conscience. The closing note — "grace, and not gold, is the best riches" — captures the Reformed emphasis on spiritual over material prosperity.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-chronicles-8.html

**Catholic (Haydock):** More sympathetic to Solomon's action regarding Pharaoh's daughter — notes she may have initially pretended conversion then relapsed; Solomon was "as yet far from communicating with infidels." Also gives alternative geographical identifications (Tadmor = Emesa, Ezion-geber = Bernice/Suez).

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-chronicles-8.html

**Critical/Conservative German Scholarship (Keil & Delitzsch):** Provides the most detailed philological and textual analysis — the *b essentiae* in v. 13, the accusative use of *sûr* in v. 15, the resolution of the 250 vs. 550 supervisors, and the identification that the two biblical accounts are "mutually supplementary extracts."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/2-chronicles-8.html

**Anglican (Ellicott):** Gives balanced historical-grammatical notes with careful attention to cross-references in Kings and geographical identification, plus a thoughtful resolution of the shipping logistics question (v. 18).

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/8.htm

---

*Note: No distinctively Lutheran (LCMS / 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan (Seedbed / Wesley Center), Eastern Orthodox (OCA), or modern scholarly (Bible Odyssey / NET Bible) commentary on this specific chapter was located within the allowed site searches. The Baptist Garner-Howes commentary referred readers to its 1 Kings 9 notes without adding separate material.*
